statement: After congestion pricing began on 5 January 2025, daily NO2 and PM2.5 at EPA regulatory monitors inside the Congestion Relief Zone fell relative to monitors elsewhere in New York City.

graph_evidence.note: No road-pricing findings in the graph (see mob-crz-traffic). The traffic-to-pollutant link is thin: traffic-related pollution -> NO2 has 1 finding; traffic -> particulates and traffic -> NO2 return no relationship. The downstream health link is dense:

graph_evidence.summary: 91 ratio findings; 78 above 1, 12 below; 59 with CI above 1, 7 with CI below 1; median ratio 1.16 (mixed increments and designs)
157 ratio findings; 144 above 1, 9 below; 88 with CI above 1, 4 with CI below 1; median ratio 1.15 (mixed increments and designs)
49 ratio findings; 46 above 1, 3 below; 35 with CI above 1, 0 with CI below 1; median ratio 1.51 (mixed increments and designs)

literature.citation: Johansson C, Burman L, Forsberg B (2009). The effects of congestions tax on air quality and health. Atmos Environ 43:4843-4854.
literature.finding: Modelled NOx emissions in inner Stockholm fell 8.5%, PM10 emissions about 13%; concentration changes were smaller.

literature.citation: Kelly F et al. (2011). The impact of the congestion charging scheme on air quality in London. HEI Research Report 155.
literature.finding: Little detectable change in measured NOx, NO2 or PM10 attributable to the London charge.

literature.citation: Simeonova E, Currie J, Nilsson P, Walker R (2021). Congestion pricing, air pollution, and children's health. J Human Resources 56(4):971-996.
literature.finding: Stockholm charge lowered ambient pollution 5-15% and acute asthma visits of young children.

literature.citation: Fraser T, Park YG, Lu D, Tayarani M, Deng H, Gao HO (2025). A first look into congestion pricing in the United States: PM2.5 impacts after six months of New York City cordon pricing. npj Clean Air 1:39.
literature.finding: Daily maximum PM2.5 in the CRZ fell 3.05 ug/m3 (22%) against a counterfactual, Jan-Jun 2025, 42 monitors (press coverage; paper not read in full).

literature.citation: NYC DOHMH (14 August 2026). Congestion pricing air quality report.
literature.finding: PM2.5, NO2, NO and black carbon in the CBD were not significantly different from the no-toll counterfactual in 2025 (secondary report).

prediction.magnitude: Two-way fixed-effects DiD (site and date effects) of log daily NO2, in-zone vs other NYC monitors, 2025 vs 2022-2024: -3% to -10%. Same for PM2.5: 0% to -8%. The research disagrees on PM2.5, so the PM2.5 prediction is weaker than the NO2 prediction.
prediction.support_if: NO2 DiD below 0 with a 95% interval below 0 (the primary test). PM2.5 is secondary.
prediction.refute_if: NO2 DiD at or above 0 with an interval that excludes -3%.

plan: Data: EPA AQS pre-generated daily files (aqs.epa.gov/aqsweb/airdata), NO2 parameter 42602 and PM2.5 parameter 88101, years 2022-2025, sites in the five NYC counties (FIPS 36005, 36047, 36061, 36081, 36085). In-zone: New York County sites south of 60th Street (by the site's latitude and the CRZ boundary). Adjacent: Manhattan north of 60th St, reported separately. Comparison: the other boroughs. Daily site mean of the primary monitor (POC averaged). Model: log(conc) ~ site FE + date FE + inzone x post, post = from 5 Jan 2025. Date effects absorb weather and regional transport common to the city. Interval: block bootstrap by ISO week (1,000 draws). Placebo: post = 5 Jan 2024 on 2022-2024. A secondary check uses the DOHMH NYCCAS annual averages by UHF if a 2025 value is published. Figure: monthly in-zone minus comparison log difference with the start date marked. Design limits: few in-zone sites (likely one or two), so the result is a site-level comparison, not a zone average; regional PM2.5 dominates local traffic PM2.5.
alternatives: Regional background change (wildfire smoke in 2023, transported sulfate) — absorbed by date effects only if it is spatially uniform
Local construction or site-specific changes near a single in-zone monitor
Long-run decline in vehicle emissions that is faster in Manhattan (fleet turnover, bus electrification)
Traffic diverted to highways near comparison monitors (e.g. Cross Bronx) raises the comparison and inflates the DiD
